subject: research/watchdog-twin
professional: a reliability / communications engineer who sizes supervisory timeouts on lossy links (burst-error channel modelling, run-length statistics, weakly-hard real-time), plus an applied probabilist for the run-length mathematics. They would check first that the mean time to a run of m losses is right, that the i.i.d.-vs-bursty gap is not just an obvious consequence of the assumed channel, and whether a Gilbert fit to real telemetry is addressed.

evidence.correctness: Recomputed independently with numpy (absorbing-Markov-chain fundamental-matrix solve, np.linalg.solve(I-Q,1), stationary start; not the author's rational back-substitution). Real-link mean time to trip at p=0.05, m=5: L=2 637.100, L=5 235.391, L=10 286.332, L=20 453.095, L=50 987.666 (results.txt: 637.1, 235.4, 286.3, 453.1, 987.7). Twin (1-p^m)/((1-p)p^m) = 3.36842e6 (3.368e6). Worst burst length for m=5 by grid search over L: 5.15 (README 5.15). Closed forms: m_real continuous at L=10, target 1e6: 81.84 (paper 81.8); e*m/p >= 1e6 gives m = 1e6*0.05/e = 18394 (paper 18394). Ratio range 3.4e6/987.7 = 3.4e3 to 1.43e4 (README 3.4e3 to 1.4e4). Every checked number matched to the printed precision. 8 numbers checked, no discrepancy. Run via python3 on the whole chain, plus the repo's own test comparing exact against enumeration of all paths.
evidence.completeness: Claims checked: (1) exact twin and real mean time to trip: works, tests plus results.txt; (2) non-monotone in L with argmin near m: results.txt section 3 and my grid; (3) large-m rate approximation within 1.2% / 0.15%: test_rate_approximations_converge passes; (4) m for a target mean time, and unknown-L worst case m=192 and 18394: present in results.txt lines 49-50; (5) Monte Carlo cross-check: line 53 (232.3 vs 235.4, ratio 0.987, a 1.3% gap, said to be sampling error but not shown with a standard error); (6) live page and svg exist (figure script, false_trip.svg). README says 12 tests about 5 s: true (12 tests, 3.3 s). Ran experiments/run.py? No (about 2 min); I recomputed the cells instead. Not done and stated: no link traces, no windowed/adaptive watchdog, no Gilbert-Elliott. No stubs or TODOs found.
evidence.verification: Ran PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v: 12 tests OK. Mutations (each reverted, git status clean afterwards): M1 drop one iteration of the back-substitution loop (range(m-2)): 4 failures, caught. M3 remove the 1/(1-p) in gilbert_params a: 4 failures, caught. M4 simulate_first_trip run>=m changed to run>m: 1 failure, caught (Monte Carlo test). M2 constant in m_twin_approx (target*(1-p)*2): 12/12 still pass, not caught (the twin-side timeout approximation is only exercised through min_m, not compared to its closed form at a tight tolerance). The exact core, the parameterisation and the simulator are all guarded by independent checks (enumeration, survival sum, DP, Monte Carlo); one auxiliary approximation is not. Score 3.
evidence.craft: Read src/watchdog_twin/model.py (132 lines), tests/test_model.py (101), experiments/run.py (81). Clean pure-Python module, exact Fractions where float elimination would cancel (values reach 1e13), docstring states the derivation, infeasible (p, L) raises ValueError, b=1 returns inf deliberately. Defects: gilbert_params computes a before validating p (p=1 gives ZeroDivisionError rather than ValueError); real_mtt returns float(Fraction) from p and L converted from floats so Fraction(a) carries float rounding noise (immaterial, verified by matching my independent solve); no_trip_prob is O(N*m) with sum(B[1:m]) in the inner loop, fine for tests; simulate_first_trip's cap silently returns 10**7 on a censored run, biasing Monte Carlo downward for large m with no flag; empty __init__.py; no type hints.
evidence.claims: Each headline number in the README and paper traces to results.txt and matched my recomputation. Limits are stated frankly in both: stylised, no link traces, loss exactly 0/1 by state, p fixed at 0.05, bare consecutive-miss counter, and the twin 'is a deliberately naive baseline: one fitted to the burst length reproduces the real values by construction', which is the honest admission that the headline contrast is a consequence of the model. Attribution to Gilbert 1960 and Elliott 1963 is right; the CU Boulder groups are named as direction only, with an explicit non-affiliation statement. Weakness: the title says a twin 'says a watchdog almost never false-trips' as if a finding about twins in general, whereas it is a statement about one deliberately mis-specified twin; the 'sooner by 3.4e3 to 1.4e4' ratios are presented as striking when they are the expected gap between a memoryless and a bursty model of the same p. The abstract is a single dense paragraph.
evidence.fitness: A robotics engineer sizing a watchdog can use the m-versus-L table and the e*m/p worst-case rule directly: the walk-through (pick target 1e6 ticks, read off m for L unknown) works, and the exact solver is usable on a fitted (p, L). But as research it is a re-derivation. Nearest prior work: the mean waiting time for a run of m failures in a Markov-dependent sequence is classical run-length theory (Feller vol. 1 ch. XIII for i.i.d., Markov extensions in Fu-Koutras 1994 and the Markov-chain-embedding literature, Balakrishnan-Koutras 'Runs and Scans'); Gilbert-Elliott burst error statistics and run-of-loss distributions are textbook in communications (Yajnik et al. 1999 'Measurement and modelling of the temporal dependence in packet loss' gives consecutive-loss statistics from real traces); and consecutive-miss tolerance for control loops is the weakly-hard real-time literature (Bernat-Burns-Llamosi 2001, (m,K) constraints; Hespanha-Naghshtabrizi-Xu 2007 on networked control with dropouts). The e*m/p worst-burst rule and the adaptive-worst-L argument (a timeout cannot be sized from p alone) are neat and I did not find them stated this way, but they are an easy corollary. No real telemetry; no estimator of (p, L) from logs. Score 2: sound and useful as an application note, not a publishable result.
evidence.domain: A reliability engineer would accept the Gilbert model as the standard first burst-loss model, the exact absorbing-chain computation, the stationary start, and the warning that timeouts need a burst-length estimate from logs. They would ask for: a Gilbert-Elliott channel (partial loss in the good state, the real-world norm: Yajnik et al. find loss in both states), a k-of-n windowed watchdog, which is the usual industrial mitigation and the thing the paper lists as future work, and a mixture over L rather than a worst case. They would also note that for p=0.05 at 50 Hz the monitored link is far lossier than typical for a supervised robot link. Method sound, limits honest, departs from practice by testing only the bare counter.

defects.what: Novelty is overstated by framing: the i.i.d. twin versus bursty real gap follows by construction (the paper says so), and the run-time mathematics, burst-loss model and consecutive-miss tolerance are classical (Feller, Markov run theory, Gilbert-Elliott, Yajnik 1999, weakly-hard (m,K) constraints). None is cited beyond Gilbert and Elliott.
Seeded bug in m_twin_approx (constant factor 2 inside the log) passes all 12 tests: the closed-form timeout rule for the twin is untested against its exact counterpart.
simulate_first_trip returns the cap (1e7) for censored runs without any flag, biasing Monte Carlo means low for large m.
gilbert_params computes a before checking p<1, so p=1 raises ZeroDivisionError instead of the documented ValueError.
Monte Carlo check (232.3 vs exact 235.4) reported as a ratio only, with no standard error, so 'agrees' cannot be judged from the file.

verdict: A small, correct, honestly scoped piece of work. I recomputed eight headline numbers (five real-link mean times to trip, the twin value, the worst burst length, the 18394 bound and the closed-form timeout) with an absorbing-chain solve the author did not write, and every one matched. Tests are good: 12 pass, and three of four seeded bugs (loop length, parameterisation, simulator threshold) were caught; one auxiliary approximation was not. It is finished as scoped and its limits are stated, including that the contrast is built into a deliberately naive twin. As research it is an application note: the run-length mathematics is classical and uncited beyond Gilbert and Elliott, there is no real telemetry or log-based estimator, and the natural industrial remedy (k-of-n windows, Gilbert-Elliott) is left as future work, so it is far from the PhD-level programme bar. Meets the bar: yes (correctness 4, claims 3, verification 3, median 3). Finished: yes.
